articles.text: Piedmont High School sophomore Mikey Swei won the 2025 VEX Worlds Robotics Championship in Dallas, Texas on May 8 with teammate Jacob Jung, a senior at Dublin High. Swei’s team, Double Play, and their alliance partners, Jackson Area Robotics, outlasted a field of 800 teams to become the high school world champions. There are 11,400 VEX high school teams world-wide, and Swei’s team qualified for the World Championship by winning a tournament in January held in Salt Lake City, Utah. Double Play made it through the qualifying rounds in Dallas and was the No. 1 seed going into the single elimination Championship playoffs. In the finals, Double Play and its alliance partner competed a best of three match. It lost the first but won Round Two to stay alive. In the pivotal rubber match. The robot Swei constructed in Piedmont and the alliance partner’s machine outscored their two opponents to win the VEX World Championship. “Our strategy was based around securing the doubled corner points, and then the very high climbing robot climbing up to the tier three of the ladder,” said Swei.

articles.text: Progress on Piedmont’s longawaited community pool has stalled again, with the previously announced June 2 completion date now quietly pushed back. The city has not provided a new target date, saying that construction is expected to finish sometime this summer. The project’s $34.9 million budget remains unchanged, funded by $25.1 million in Measure UU bonds and associated interest. The last formal update came at the March 3 City Council meeting, when officials projected a June 2 construction end date. Now, city staff say a more detailed timeline will be shared at the next council update, scheduled for July 7. Work still to be completed includes deck work, concrete pours, and exterior finishes. Once the site is built out and the pools are filled with water, the facility will enter a “commissioning” period—at least four weeks of testing critical systems like the electric heat pump. An opening date will be announced only after this process is underway. The facility will also need to obtain approval permits from Alameda County Environmental Health prior to opening. One factor contributing to recent delays is the unexpected death of project executive George Sanen of Griffin Structures. Joshua Kaiser has stepped in as the new project executive and will oversee the remainder of the build. Kaiser brings more than 25 years of experience managing complex public construction projects and has assumed full leadership. Griffin Structures President Jon Hughes will remain involved to provide continuity. According to the city, Sanen’s name will be included on the final facility signage honoring key staff and officials who contributed to the project. articles.text: Piedmont’s Park Commission will be discussing the landscaping and open space components of the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan at their meeting tonight at 5:30 p.m. in Piedmont City Hall. The presentation and discussion will focus on elements of the Specific Plan that relate to the Park Commission’s charge, addressing proposed improvements to the public realm, preservation of significant open space and scenic views, and wildfire safety provisions. The Park Commission presentation is part of a series of public discussions of the draft Housing Plan, which began with two City Council study sessions in April. Additional planned meetings include: • June 18, 2025: Recreation Commission • August-September 2025: Public hearings at Planning Commission and City Council For those unable to attend, meeting video and presentation materials will be available on the project website after the meeting. New Multifamily Housing in Moraga Canyon The product of in-depth study and community engagement beginning in summer 2023, the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan outlines a vision for a new neighborhood in Moraga Canyon that would: • bring new housing to Piedmont, creating opportunities for people of all income levels • • • enhance recreational amenities through an expanded sports field and new hiking trail improve road safety, with a new bike lane, sidewalks, and traffic signal at Red Rock Road model best practices in wildfire resistant construction and landscaping The Draft Specific Plan details development locations, site improvements, and infrastructure requirements for the construction up to 199 units of new housing on City-owned land in Moraga Canyon, 60 of which would be affordable to lower income households. The document anticipates development of multifamily residential buildings between four and six stories and includes two options for where these buildings could be located – either on the north side or the south side of Moraga Avenue. articles.text: From the music of Grease to Gustav Holst’s Jupiter performed recently by Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School musicians, an inspiring musical celebration capped the school year. But the school district’s sterling music program is now being threatened. Recently, the school board approved a program to end instrumental music education for fourth graders next year, a move that is short-sighted and will limit the musical potential of our students. Learning an instrument takes time, and it requires repeated hands-on practice to become proficient enough to play more than just “Hot Cross Buns.” Delaying instrumental music education to 5th grade means that students will have less of an opportunity to master an instrument, and this could have a major impact on middle school and high school band and orchestra. Students also lose out on all the cognitive benefits that come from learning an instrument. Current and recent elementary and middle school students have complained about a challenging and frustrating music experience. Instead of fixing this problem — such as hiring a full-time music teacher, asking for parent volunteers, or incorporating other kinds of classroom support — the school board threw the baby out with the bathwater. Next year, our fourth graders will get 60 minutes a week of “theater arts” in a program that has yet to be defined or developed. The school board heralded this as an exciting change. While we love theater and all that it offers for kids, we don’t understand why it must come at the expense of music. There are plenty of ways to incorporate theater arts into our classrooms – indeed, many of our elementary teachers have already done this – but there are very few opportunities for students to try a variety of instruments and perform in groups. Now they won’t have that chance until 5th grade. Next year has been called a “bridge year.” This only adds to the uncertainty around the future of Piedmont’s music program. Furthermore, this change was made with little transparency and was unnecessarily rushed. Parents and students were scolded for raising their concerns, and there was a fallacy about the collaboration of teachers and staff. Our neighboring school districts – including Berkeley, Orinda, Lafayette, and Moraga – introduce instruments in the fourth grade, and with regression such as this, we will continue to lose students to private schools. With this shift, our district is not being innovative. It is taking a step back in the musical education it offers to our students. articles.text: Piedmont City Council held the first of two public hearings on Piedmont’s proposed FY2025-26 budget at their regular meeting on Monday, June 2. City Council is expected to adopt the budget following a second public hearing on June 16. The budget, adopted annually, serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to finance its services and infrastructure in the coming year. This year’s budget was presented by retired Finance Director Michael Szczech, performing interim duties while the City awaits the arrival of its next appointed Finance Director, Kiran Bawa. The proposed FY2025-26 budget aims to maintain existing service levels citywide, prioritizing high quality service delivery, fiscal responsibility, and planning for the future while bringing several multi-year major projects to completion, including the City’s new community pool, 9-1-1 dispatch center relocation, and the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The proposed budget features a General Fund of $40 million. A $8.3 million spending plan for the Facilities Capital Fund is also included for work on finishing projects such as the community pool, dispatch center, and more. The budget hearing reported a current projection with expected revenue $1.2 million above the current year’s budget and expenditures expected to be lower than budgeted by $1.6 million. With an expected surplus around $3.6 million, City staff recommended that $850,000 of it be transferred from the General Fund to the City’s Equipment fund, keeping the remainder for next year’s budget. Frank Ryan, Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee chair, spoke at Monday’s budget hearing. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee’s written report to Council endorses the proposed plan, stating: “The proposed budget for FY 25-26 reflects the City’s continued commitment to conservative budgeting and financial discipline. This approach ensures that the City can continue to provide high quality public services, replace aging equipment, and address infrastructure repairs, while retaining a strong General Fund.” Looking forward, the Committee’s letter encourages the City to further quantify and plan for future infrastructure costs. The Committee also reiterates their call from previous reports for the City to explore options for additional revenue sources, including an increase in the Transfer Tax. Community Feedback Several community members spoke at Monday’s Council meeting to urge the City Council to include money in the budget for an additional crossing guard at the intersection of Requa Road and Wildwood Avenue. “We want to thank the City so far for being really helpful. Everything’s been really well received – the director of Public Works has come out and met with us – and yet I still don’t feel comfortable with the solutions that we have in place and how the street exists today going forward,” said parent Nelly Thornton. “...It’s just that the intersection is very unusual and needs someone there to help navigate and make this street and what we see on a daily basis safer.” The passionate parents estimated the cost of hiring a crossing guard at about $25,000, which they assert is a small addition to a budget of $40 million. The next FY2025-26 budget hearing will continue in City Council chambers on Monday, June 16.
articles.title: City Council considers proposed 2025-26 Budget

articles.text: For many students, summer means turning off the alarm, sleeping late, and enjoying an unstructured day. While freedom from the routine of the academic year provides a mentally refreshing break, summer is a great time to practice executive functioning and life skills. Becoming more competent at managing the logistics of life carries over into improved academics and increased confidence. Here are three simple ways kids can work on these important life skills: Field trip fun day Give your kids the opportunity to plan a fun day out to a local museum or outdoor activity. They can research opening times, entry fees, and transport logistics. Will you drive or take BART? Public transportation is a fantastic way to practice realworld skills like reading a schedule, determining fares, and navigating public spaces. By giving kids control over this activity, they are invested in making it a fun day for everyone. Plan and cook a simple meal Cooking requires a tremendous amount of executive functioning. From planning ingredient lists to carving out time to go to the grocery store to understanding how to time different meal components so everything is ready simultaneously is a big learning curve. The multiple steps involved in cooking can be overwhelming, so starting simple and age-appropriate can help build these skills and grow confidence. Pack your bags Regardless of if your child is going to day camp or on a vacation, give them the opportunity to pack their own bag. Not only can they have the experience of thinking through what they might need for different weather conditions or activities, they can also think about what food and drink they might want. You can help them be aware of any restrictions — like liquids on airlines or allergens at camp — they need to consider. While it takes time and patience to let kids pack their own bags, remember that independence for them is independence for you. Using the summer to practice executive functioning skills gives your child the opportunity to build cognitive pathways that correlate with better academic performance during the school year. articles.text: Sophomore is 2 seconds away from school record Piedmont High sophomore Sebastien Swain, the only member of the track team to qualify for the State Championships, came within two seconds of setting a school record in the 800 meters. Competing at Veterans Memorial Stadium at Buchanan High School in Clovis on Friday, May 30, he posted a time of 1:53.15, two seconds off the Piedmont school record set by Gordon Johnson in 1988. Competing at State pits together hundreds of California’s top runners along with their family and friends into the large high school stadium. It’s a championship atmosphere unlike almost every high school track event. “It’s definitely a special meet,” said Swain. “I’m just super happy Sebastien Swain’s CIF State Championship marks his third State Championship appearance and first for the track team. Sebastien Swain is less than two seconds behind Gordon Johnson’s 1988 school record of 1:51.69 in the 800. Sophomore Sebastien Swain (#6) represented Piedmont at the 2025 CIF State Championship, finishing the 800 meters in 18th. to make it there. You have the atmosphere, all the people, and the opportunity to see what you can do against the top runners in the state. I’m just a sophomore, so it’s a chance to see what it takes and what I need to do to match up with my competition.” Swain placed 18th in a field of 29 half milers. “Because I’m racing all these fast people, my goal was to just put myself in a good position. I wanted to get out early so I’m not stuck at the back early in the race. I wanted to come through to the line one a second faster than I normally would,” Swain said. Though a sophomore, Swain has now completed the third CIF State Championship of his running career. He qualified for State in the fall for two years on the cross-country team. “It’s exciting. I’m looking forward to building off this success and maybe next year, not just qualify for State, but to actually place in the finals. That’s my plan,” he added. With a personal record time of 1:53.15, Swain is less than two seconds back of Gordon Johnson’s 1988 record of 1:51.69. Swain is well-aware that he’s nipping at Gordon’s heals with two years of eligibility left. “Oh, I’m thinking about it; Gordon’s going down,” Swain said with a laugh. “My mom and my dad actually know Gordon. He’s still around Piedmont, so it’s really neat to have that connection,” he added. Swain also won the Western Alameda County Conference title in the 1600 at the league championship on May 9. He opted to only compete in the 800 at the NCS’ Bayshore Area Championship and Meet of Champions. “The 800 has definitely been my focus. In order to run a 1600 well and close, you have to run a good 800. I felt a good way to improve in the 1600 was to get the shorter distance down. It also had to do with working on the short-end because that’s more difficult. I know I can run with endurance, especially after cross country. As the season progressed, I dealt with an injury that made long aerobic fitness more difficult. Because I wasn’t getting that work in, it made more sense to focus on the 800.” Swain said. Now entering the summer, Swain will return to toe the line in the fall for the cross country season.
articles.title: Swain sets PR in 800 at CIF State Championship

articles.text: The original article was written by Owen Blanford, then a Bronco division player and 5th grader at Havens Elementary School. It first appeared in the Piedmont Post in May 2018 and has been updated with the 2025 Award recipients. Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation (PBSF) is proud to be a community league dedicated to providing opportunities for players of all skill levels. PBSF’s mission emphasizes that the games are an opportunity to learn life lessons and skills that have meaning beyond the game of baseball or softball, such as sportsmanship, character, confidence, resilience, being part of a team, and building memories that last a lifetime. Former PBSF President Murray Davis was instrumental in the development of the PBSF mission with his own youth baseball experience as his personal guide. Murray played youth baseball with hall-of-famer Robin Yount. While Murray didn’t have the same skills of the future hall of famer, Murray was fond of telling anyone that his love of the game helped Robin Yount fulfill his achievements in baseball. Former PBSF Board member Barry Barnes said, “Every time I asked, ‘how are you doing, Murray?’ His response was almost always, ‘I’m living the dream man, living the dream.’” Murray carried the positive attitude from youth baseball throughout his life. After his passing in late 2012, PBSF created the “Livin’ the Dream” award in his honor. The “Livin’ the Dream” award is given to one player on each team. The award is not a MVP award, rather is given to a player who embodies positive, intangible contributions to the team, sportsmanship, perseverance, and a positive infectious attitude. It’s like giving the award to a person who is most like Murray Davis. When Former PBSF President Chris Hart gave out the “Livin’ the Dream” award he looked for a player who enjoyed playing on the team and whose teammates enjoyed with him, who gave full effort and a player who showed a desire to improve.
articles.title: Baseball, Softball Foundation announces winners of Murray Davis Livin’ the Dream Awards

Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation (PBSF) is proud to be a community league dedicated to providing opportunities for players of all skill levels. PBSF’s mission emphasizes that the games are an opportunity to learn life lessons and skills that have meaning beyond the game of baseball or softball, such as sportsmanship, character, confidence, resilience, being part of a team, and building memories that last a lifetime. Former PBSF President Murray Davis was instrumental in the development of the PBSF mission with his own youth baseball experience as his personal guide. Murray played youth baseball with hall-of-famer Robin Yount. While Murray didn’t have the same skills of the future hall of famer, Murray was fond of telling anyone that his love of the game helped Robin Yount fulfill his achievements in baseball. Former PBSF Board member Barry Barnes said, “Every time I asked, ‘how are you doing, Murray?’ His response was almost always, ‘I’m living the dream man, living the dream.’” Murray carried the positive attitude from youth baseball throughout his life. After his passing in late 2012, PBSF created the “Livin’ the Dream” award in his honor. The “Livin’ the Dream” award is given to one player on each team. articles.text: Bancroft Garden curator Brian Kemble Join Ruth Bancroft Gardens curator Brian Kemble this Saturday, June 7, in a guided tour of the garden’s unique spring blooms. Visitors will get a closer look at columnar, barrel, and Opuntia (paddle) cacti and learn more about their short but spectacular flowering stages. Kemble has worked with the gardens for 45 years and oversees thousands of cacti and succulent species that grow in the garden’s three acres. As curator, he is in charge of hybridizing plants and finding two plants that have complementary characteristics and combining them to create new species. Kemble worked closely with Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, who was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Kemble will share Bancroft’s legacy with tour attendees and offer his decades of firsthand experience, having traveled extensively through the U.S., Mexico, and Chile in search of wild cactus populations. The garden will also be hosting a pop-up sale of unique cacti. Artisan crafts and refreshments will be available for purchase. The tour begins at 12:30 p.m. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/cactuscrawl-guided-tour-with-our-curator/ to learn more and to register.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony has announced its 2025–26 season, featuring four dynamic symphonic programs and four intimate chamber music performances. Following the conclusion of Music Director Joseph Young’s successful six-year tenure, Berkeley Symphony will welcome an exceptional lineup of conductors to the podium for a season that promises to be both innovative and inspiring. “This season represents an exciting new chapter for Berkeley Symphony,” said Executive Director Marion Atherton. “We’re thrilled to welcome some of today’s most compelling conductors, each bringing their unique artistic vision to our stage. For the 2025–26 season, we’re excited to shine a light on stirring masterpieces from the classical canon alongside groundbreaking contemporary works. From Dvořák’s lyrical Eighth Symphony to Shostakovich’s spirited Ninth and Haydn’s vivid ‘Military’ Symphony, we’re exploring rich musical territory beyond the standard repertoire while showcasing the versatility and excellence of our orchestra.” New subscription packages are available now. Returning subscribers may renew online, by mail, or by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800. Individual concert tickets will go on sale in mid-July. All Symphonic Series concerts will be held at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley; all Chamber Series concerts will take place at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Symphonic Series The Symphonic Series opens with Visions of Elysium on Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025, at 4 p.m. Guest conductor Dina Gilbert, currently principal conductor of Les Grands Ballets Canadiens, associate conductor of the Orchestre symphonique de Montréal, and music director of the Walla Walla Symphony, will make her Berkeley Symphony debut. Known for her “contagious dynamism and audacious programming,” Gilbert will lead a powerful program featuring Beethoven’s monumental Symphony No. 3, Eroica, and Samy Moussa’s ethereal Elysium for Orchestra. The series continues with Refracted Light on Sunday, Oct. 5, 2025, at 4 p.m. Edwin Outwater, described by Michael Tilson Thomas as “one of the most innovative conductors on the scene today,” will lead the orchestra. Violinist Helen Kim is featured as soloist in Samuel Adams’ textured Chamber Concerto. The program also includes Yaz Lancaster’s Gender Envy and Haydn’s celebratory Symphony No. 100, Military. On Sunday, Nov. 16, 2025, at 4 p.m., Ming Luke will conduct Worlds Beyond, a program exploring reflection and transformation. Luke, noted for his “energy, creativity, and charisma,” opens with the West Coast premiere of Juan Pablo Contreras’ Alma Monarca, co-commissioned by Berkeley Symphony. Soprano Laquita Mitchell makes her Berkeley Symphony debut in Strauss’s evocative Four Last Songs. The evening continues with Missy Mazzoli’s cosmic Sinfonia (for Orbiting Spheres) and concludes with Shostakovich’s spirited Symphony No. 9. The symphonic season concludes with Fables and Folklore on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026, at 4 p.m. Internationally acclaimed conductor Carolyn Kuan, known for her “extraordinary versatility, innovative programming, and dedication to contemporary music,” will lead a program inspired by cultural traditions from around the world. Guitarist Marc Teicholz will perform Clarice Assad’s colorful Concerto for Guitar and Chamber Orchestra, O Saci-Pererê. The program also includes Huang Ruo’s vibrant Folk Songs for Orchestra and Dvořák’s lush Symphony No. 8. Chamber Series The Chamber Series begins with Roots and Resonances on Sunday, Feb. 22, 2026, at 4 p.m. Curated by acclaimed composer Samuel Adams, the concert features percussionist Haruka Fujii alongside a Berkeley Symphony string quartet in works that explore texture and timbre. The program includes music by Salina Fisher and Osvaldo Golijov, as well as Haruka Fujii’s Divisions and Adams’ Sundial. The series continues with French Connections, curated by Dianne Nicolini, the voice of Classical California KDFC, on Sunday, March 22, 2026, at 4 p.m. The concert will feature works by Francis Poulenc and Lili Boulanger, along with Gabriel Fauré’s Piano Quartet No. 1 in C minor. On Sunday, April 12, 2026, at 4 p.m., composer Juan Pablo Contreras—also featured in this season’s Symphonic Series— curates The Music of Muses, a program exploring artistic inspiration. In addition to works by Reena Esmail, Jennifer Higdon, and Bedřich Smetana, the concert will include Contreras’ own Musas Mexicanas, a tribute to three influential Mexican women who helped shape the country’s history. The Chamber Series concludes with I, Too, Sing America on Sunday, May 31, 2026, at 4 p.m., curated by James Parrish Smith, organist and music director of Berkeley’s First Presbyterian Church. The program features works by Brian Raphael Nabors and Anna Clyne—both past collaborators with Berkeley Symphony—as well as Dvořák’s seminal “American” String Quartet. About Berkeley Symphony For more than 50 years, Berkeley Symphony has established itself as a cultural cornerstone of the East Bay through its commitment to artistic excellence, community engagement, and introducing audiences to new and lesser-known works. Berkeley Symphony takes pride in crafting thoughtfully balanced programs that pair contemporary voices with beloved classics, creating meaningful musical experiences that resonate with the East Bay’s diverse community. Ticket Information Subscriptions to the Symphonic Series and the Chamber Series are on sale now. For the Symphonic Series, four-concert subscriptions range from $48 to $280. The Chamber Series subscriptions are $120. Subscriptions can be purchased by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800 or visiting berkeleysymphony.org.

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) newest exhibition Students on Strike highlights the 1968 student-led strike at San Francisco State University (SFSU) and other noteworthy movements that established the nation’s first Black Studies Department and first College of Ethnic Studies at the university. The exhibition features historical and contemporary posters and photographs to draw comparisons between the strike at SFSU and the recent campus protests against the war in Gaza. In October 2024, San Francisco University State University students protested the Israel-Hamas war and the statewide school system’s ongoing investments in weapons manufacturers. Student-led demonstrations were seen at campuses across the state and at University of California schools. Museum visitors will be presented with an opportunity to integrate local historical context with more recent student strikes. Students on Strike is on view through May 31, 2026. Visit https://museumca.org/ on-view/students-on-strike/ to learn more. The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA)

articles.text: Photo by Jeremy Daniel Broadway In Chicago’s production of “A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical,” stars Hannah Jewel Kohn and Nick Fradiani. The smash-hit musical and biographical drama A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical is now playing at San Francisco’s Golden Gate Theatre for a limited engagement through Sunday, June 22. Created in collaboration with singer-songwriter Neil Diamond himself, the musical tells the true story of a kid from Brooklyn’s meteoric rise to fame and how he became an American rock icon. “Some of my most thrilling nights have been while I was on tour, bringing my music to audiences across the world,” said Diamond. “Having A Beautiful Noise go on tour is an honor and I can’t wait for audiences across North America to experience this show. I hope they enjoy it as much as I have.” Including a catalogue of classics like “America,” “Forever in Blue Jeans,” and “Sweet Caroline,” Diamond’s story is portrayed by Nick Fradiani, who. played the title role in “American Idol” in 2015 and has since released his debut album “Hurricane” featuring the hit single “Beautiful Life.” Joining Fradiani are Tony Nominee Robert Westenberg (Neil Diamond – Now), Hannah Jewel Kohn (Marcia Murphey), Lisa Reneé Pitts (Doctor), Michael Accardo (Bert Berns/ Kieve Diamond), Tuck Milligan (Fred Weintraub/ Tommy O’Rourke), Kate A. Mulligan (Ellie Greenwich/ Rose Diamond) and Tiffany Tatreau(Jaye Posner). The show is produced by Ken Davenport and Bob Gaudio. “I couldn’t imagine a more perfect way to honor [Diamond’s] legacy than having A Beautiful Noise touring North America, visiting the same cities where he gave so many people so much joy,” Davenport said. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.broadwaysf.com/ events/a-beautiful-noise/golden-gate-theatre/calendar.

articles.text: Bear Valley Music Festival begins July 18, marking the 56th anniversary of the iconic, eclectic music festival along Highway 4 that brings together renowned artists and ensembles from various genres, including classical, jazz, rock, pop and more. The annual summer event is held in the picturesque Bear Valley nestled within the Sierra Nevada Mountains. All concerts are tucked inside an outdoor tent that holds over 500 guests This year’s lineup features an eclectic variety of music from 80’s tribute bands to classic jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy,” said Board of Directors president Julia Mee. “From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone.” Queen Nation, a Queen tribute band, kicks off the music festival with a performance on Friday, July 18. They are followed on Saturday by San Francisco’s Super Diamond, A Neil Diamond tribute band, delivering a dazzling show of Neil Diamond‘s hits from “Sweet Caroline” to “I Am…I Said.” After a week of tribute bands, the festival offers a performance of Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony on Friday, July 25. The program includes guitarist Lyle Sheffler performing Spanish composer Joaquin Rodrigo’s evocative Concierto de Aranjuez, plus a piece by the relatively unknown 18th-century composer Marianna Martines. The July 27 program features music by Mozart and Haydn interspersed with contemporary pop tunes. A symphonic finale consists of the music of Leonard Bernstein, Erich Wolfgang Korngold, and Sergei Rachmaninoff on Friday, August 1. Bear Valley Music Festival’s annual gala event is on Saturday, August 2. Guests are invited to sport their finest period attire from the late 19th to early 20th century for an evening filled with music from that era. Gala ticket purchases include concert admission, a welcome glass of champagne or the evening’s themed cocktail, dinner with wine, and a live auction. Soprano Carrie Hennessey closes out this year’s festival on Sunday, August 3. Back by popular demand after last summer’s performance, Hennessey returns to perform favorite songs from Broadway and Hollywood, including music from Les Miserable, Lion King and The Sound of Music. articles.text: Shutter Island, just off the coast of Massachusetts, is a federal maximum-security prison for the criminally insane. In the opening scene of Martin Scorsese’s film, Shutter Island, a small ferryboat slides out of a wispy fog and bears down on the only harbor on the island. Beyond stand dark, hunched buildings from another century. There is something foreboding, even ominous about the place, long ago named Ashecliffe Asylum. Terry Daniels (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his partner Chuck Aule (Mark Ruffalo), both United States Marshals, have been sent to the island to search for an escaped patient, Rachel Soldano (Patricia Clarkson). Immediately, as the Marshals, in the company of grim prison guards, enter through the gates of the asylum, the noir mood of the film is established and then is slowly ratcheted up. Patients stand silently watching, some raking the lawns, other tending plants. All have a chilling, vacuous look. Soon it becomes evident, through a series of flashbacks, that Daniels is struggling with demons of his own. He explains to Chuck that his wife died in a fire, a tragedy that haunts him still, causing him severe migraines. Shutter Island is a series of set pieces in which Daniels discovers that the asylum is a labyrinth of elusive truths, long corridors, and dark rooms. A force 5 hurricane Leonardo DiCaprio in Shutter Island lashes the island and strands the two marshals until ferry service can be restored. Soldandos nowhere to be found and the staff, headed by Dr. Cawley (Ben Kingsley), can offer no explanation. She has literally vanished. And so the hunt continues. There are countless moments in the film where Scorsese pays explicit homage to Alfred Hitchcock, especially to the classic North by Northwest. And there’s a shower scene with Daniels letting the water sluice over his face that mirrors Psycho. Like so many of Hitchcock’s films, Shutter Island is a psychological thriller that twists and turns growing ever more convoluted and enigmatic. The cast is superb. Clarkson delivers a powerful and understated cameo as Soldando. Max Von Sydow, an extraordinary character actor, portrays a psychiatrist with allusions to a Nazi past. And Ben Kingsley, as the chief physician, is, again, exceptional. It’s DiCaprio’s most powerful role since The Aviator. It’s all but impossible to say more about this film without flirting with the ending, which surprises. Shutter Island will find its core audience – cinephiles who have followed the work of Martin Scorsese over these many decades. They will not be disappointed. Shutter Island. articles.text: Felicity Jones and Eddie Redmayne in The Aeronauts When I first saw the trailer for The Aeronauts, I was immediately captivated. What evokes a sense of adventure more than a towering, colorful balloon (or better yet, a sky full of them) drifting away on invisible currents of wind? The film stars Felicity Jones as Amelia Wren, a daring balloon pilot, and Eddie Redmayne as James Glaisher, an aspiring meteorologist. Set in 1862, a time when weather prediction meant little more than stepping outside, the film promises a thrilling ascent into the unknown. Jones and Redmayne, who previously charmed audiences in The Theory of Everything, reunite here with high expectations. Their mission: to rise higher than anyone before –above 23,000 feet – aboard a striking red-and-white gas balloon. The balloon, built specifically for the film, stands 80 feet tall and 55 feet wide, with a roomy wicker basket below packed with sandbags, ropes, and scientific instruments. At launch, Wren and Glaisher are far from harmonious. He’s a meticulous, rule-bound scientist; she’s a reluctant pilot, skeptical of his gadgets and ambitions. After a brief setup, they ascend straight into a turbulent storm that sets the tone for their journey –breathtaking, but fraught with danger. As they climb to unprecedented altitudes, the temperature plummets and the air thins dangerously. No one has been this high before. While the film occasionally stalls during these airborne sequences – at times lacking dramatic tension beyond the sheer vastness of the sky – it regains momentum when the pair realizes they must descend or risk death. The valve to release gas is frozen shut, triggering a suspenseful final act that redeems the slower middle stretch. Ultimately, The Aeronauts is a visual spectacle with moments of true peril and awe. While it drifts now and then, its climactic payoff is worth the ride. The Aeronauts. Directed by Tom Harper. Starring Felicity Jones, Eddie Redmayne, Tom Courtenay. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: Benji the Hunted is a family-friendly adventure that finds its heart in the wild and delivers an engaging story for young viewers. As dogs go, Benji is extraordinary. The film opens with Benji’s trainer (Frank Inn, portraying himself) refusing to believe his beloved dog was lost at sea following a shipwreck. He hires a helicopter to search for him. Sure enough, Benji survives and washes ashore on a remote, forested island. So begins Benji’s breathtaking wilderness journey. The island turns out to be inhabited. Benji witnesses a hunter shoot a mother cougar, only to soon discover her four orphaned cubs. With unwavering loyalty, Benji takes it upon himself to protect them. After finding them shelter, he sets out to gather food. Spotting a quail roasting over a campfire near a cabin, Benji steals it for the cubs. Along the way, he faces off with the hunter again, evades a threatening wolf, and is briefly captured and tied up. One close call follows another, but Benji always manages to escape, keeping young viewers on the edge of their seats and cheering for their heroic pup. Meanwhile, Frank hasn’t stopped searching. As the helicopter reappears overhead, Benji realizes rescue may be near. Help is on the way. Benji the Hunted. Directed by Joe Camp. Starring Red Steagall, Frank Inn, Nancy Francis. 1 hr 28 min. articles.text: Saturday, June 7, 7:30 p.m. Left Coast Chamber Ensemble Left Coast Chamber Ensemble (LCCE) presents Spring Contrasts. The contrasting timbres of the violin, clarinet, and piano bring to life a vibrant variety of musical imaginations. The program includes Hannah Kendall’s Processional for solo piano, Kevin Day’s virtuosic Unquiet Waters, Mel Bonis’ lyrical Suite en Trio, Op. 59 for piano, violin, and clarinet, and selections from Roberto Sierra. The centerpiece is Béla Bartók’s Contrasts for violin, clarinet, and piano, a work written for American bandleader Benny Goodman. It incorporates Hungarian and Romanian folk music and Bulgarian rhythms. Tickets may be purchased at the door for $38/general, $18/students. Subsidized ARTS ACCESS tickets invite concertgoers to pay what they can. Advance tickets are available at $35/general and $15/student. For details visit www.leftcoastensemble.org/spring-contrasts or call 415/617-LCCE (5223). Sunday, June 8, 3:00 p.m. Breshears String Trio The Breshears String Trio will perform works by Mozart, Handel/Halvorsen, Vivaldi/Colton and von Dohnányi. The Trio consists of violinist Valery Breshears (15), violist Colin Breshears (12) and cellist Starla Breshears (17). They reside at their family home in San Pablo, California. Valery and Starla are currently members of the San Francisco Symphony Youth Orchestra. All are students at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. The family in various combinations has been performing as soloists, duets, trios and quartets for 12 years. Tickets will be available at the door or in advance at www.Brownpapertickets.com/e/6652231. The event, presented by the Ken Betts Company and Montclair Village Association, features live music, beverage tastings, family activities, and community programming. Admission is free and open to all ages. Tasting packages are available for $55 in advance or $65 at the event, and include access to samples from more than 50 craft beer, wine, and cider producers, along with a commemorative festival glass. Festival manager Jacob Cohen noted the continued collaboration with local producers. “It’s been a rare pleasure working with local breweries and wineries these last three years,” he said. With curatorial input from Farmstead Cheeses & Wines and CaDraftTech, the event showcases a range of regional beverages. Live music will be performed on the Mister Beever’s Paws & Claws stage, powered by Meet Your Core Pilates. Performers include Dos Four, Namorados Da Lua, the Khalil Abdullah Quartet, and a cast performance from the upcoming Woodminster Summer Musicals production of Anastasia. Dos Four, the festival headliner, features Cuban-American artist Leyder Chapman. Namorados Da Lua, a Bay Area band, blends Brazilian rhythms with influences from jazz, reggae, and funk. The Khalil Abdullah Quartet, led by guitarist and educator Brother Khalil, opens the festival with a jazz-infused set. New this year, the Flair Travel & Adventure Zone will offer family-friendly activities and interactive experiences related to global travel and culture. Additional programming will take place in the Play-Palooza Family Fun Zone, sponsored by F&M Bank. The Oakland Fire Department’s Random Acts Parade Rig will also be onsite. Food will be available from local chefs and vendors, with offerings ranging from Thai street food and Mexican fare to classic festival options. Montclair Village restaurants and shops will remain open during the event, and artisan vendors will be featured throughout the festival area. Get discounted drink packages today at MontclairVillage.com. The Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival in 2022 Photo credit Peter Marcus. articles.text: In mid-May, Troop 1 embarked on a kayaking and camping trip at Elkhorn Slough, one of the largest estuaries in California along the coast of Monterey Bay between Santa Cruz and Monterey. Elkhorn Slough has the highest sea otter concentration in the state, along with dozens of other aquatic species. Scouts paired up in double kayaks, and after a short lesson on kayaking, ventured out of the harbor and into the slough. While many Scouts zoomed off, a few pairs stayed behind in a small cove, sheltered from the wind. Regardless of their location, all Scouts encountered a plethora of wildlife. Rafts (groups) of otters lounged on their backs in the seagrass munching away on crabs and clams and massaging air bubbles into their fur to stay afloat. Small harmless jellyfish called Velella Velella floated along by the hundreds, blown into the slough by an unlucky wind. Seals Troop 1 Scouts ready for their kayaking adventure sped through the water, investigating the kayaks, while sea lions lounged on the beach. While exploring, the scouts in the cove saw what appeared to be a large rock in the middle of the seagrass. It turned out to be a dead seal on its back! After enjoying the beauty of the slough however, came the arduous journey back. Winds reached over 20mph and many Scouts struggled to fight the wind funneling into the Slough. Everyone eventually made their way back, tired, bedraggled, but smiling. The Scouts continued on to their campsite at Sunset Beach State Park and set up camp. Fortunately, the campsite was close to the water, so everyone was able to enjoy the beach. Some fished in the surf while others played with large pieces of driftwood they found on the beach. The Scouts enjoyed a hearty taco dinner before lighting a fire, roasting marshmallows and battling each other to see who could make the most ridiculous s’more creation possible. The next morning the Scouts packed up, ate a delicious breakfast, and set off for home. The trip was not only a memorable adventure with California sea life, but also a great bonding experience, especially for the newer Scouts, who got a warm and adventurous introduction to Troop 1. Theodore Cost is a member of Piedmont Scouts Troop 1. articles.text: Book review by Lawrence Siskind In 1868, Alexander Gardner, famous for photographing a timeworn Abraham Lincoln, traveled to Wyoming to photograph the work of six peace commissioners who were negotiating treaties with the local Indians. At Fort Laramie, Gardner posed the commissioners: three on the left and three on the right. Between them, he posed a small, dark-skinned girl. Collections of Gardner’s photographs identify the six men, all distinguished military and political leaders. But who was that girl in the middle? How did she find herself standing between the six imposing white warriors? Thomas Carlyle deemed history the story of great men. For retired Princeton professor Martha Sandweiss, history can also be the story of a small, shy girl. A self-described “truffle hunter,” Sandweiss rooted about in town libraries, school archives, and family living rooms, searching for clues about the girl in the middle. She found her. Along the way she also found a throng of others – white settlers, Indians, halfbreeds, rogues, idealists, utopians, murderers – all with their own fascinating accounts. The girl in the middle was Sophie Mousseau, known as Little Flower, the eight-year old daughter of an Oglala Lakota woman and her French Canadian husband. Sophie’s mother was wounded at Blue Water Creek in Nebraska during a bloody raid led by General William Harney in 1855. Harney’s Lakota nickname was “Woman Killer” – which tells us much about the man. After the massacre, Harney rounded up the survivors and marched them to Fort Laramie, where Sophie’s mother met and married her future father. Thirteen years after serving as the unwitting matchmaker of her parents, this same General Harney returned to Fort Laramie as a peace commissioner. As he posed with Sophie for Gardner’s photograph, he had no idea who the girl was, or how he had affected her life. In describing Harney’s life, Sandweiss introduces us to Judge Charles “Horse” Allen, who presided over an earlier trial of Harney for murdering a slave. The judge was typical of the colorful characters populating the book. According to a contemporary reporter: “The Judge’s educational advantages were certainly very limited and he never improved himself much by study, for he had but little relish for books, and his knowledge of the law was very superficial.” He also “had a taste for fights” and would “adjourn his court to go watch a good one.” Harney was acquitted. Alexander Gardner was not the first photographer to visit Fort Laramie. Two years earlier, an idealistic Quaker named Ridgeway Glover had arrived. Convinced that the Indians would not harm so earnest a visitor, he defied the locals’ warning and wandered outside the Fort alone. His body was discovered later. Reports differed on whether he had been beheaded, disemboweled, or burned, but all agreed that he had been scalped. diers who found Glover’s corpse was a Civil War veteran named Posey Ryan. A decade later, he would meet and marry Sophie, who bore him five children. Ryan left Sophie for another woman – taking all five children with him. Sophie was fortunate. After marrying the woman for whom he left Sophie, Ryan later quarreled with her over money, and shot her and a step-daughter dead in a restaurant. “I didn’t have the slightest idea of killing them when I went into the restaurant,” Posey told a friend. “But … I was mad.” What of Sophie herself? She remarried, this time to a mixed-race medicine show performer, who later served as a translator for prominent anthropologists. Sophie bore him eight children. Having brought a total of 13 children into the world, she lived out her life on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota, where she found work as a laundress at a boarding school. She took advantage of her location to learn to read and write. This is not a book for the genteel or delicate. The Indians are no more idealized than the white invaders. In 1906, Sophie’s father, embittered by Indian raids on his business, told an interviewer that the Indians “ought to be killed and burned as the whites were by them.” His Indian daughter’s reaction to this grim opinion is not reported. Nor is this a book for advocates of “intersectionality.” Minorities did not find common cause with each other. A peace commissioner’s wife hears Frederick Douglass declare that black people deserved civil rights more than Indians, because “the negro is more like the white man than the Indian in his tastes and tendencies, and disposition to accept civilization.” Professor Sandweiss narrates her story in an easy, friendly manner. She is not above leavening her reporting with literary flourishes now and then. Describing Sophie’s death, she writes: “She passed away in her simple dugout home alongside a trout stream. The bearskin hanging over her front door flapped in the winds blowing from the west.” Perhaps the bearskin flapped, but that’s prose, not history. In an age when lives were nasty, br utish, and short, Sophie’s longevity is astonishing. She survived poverty, wars, massacres, and natural disasters to live to 1936, midway through Franklin Roosevelt’s second term. General Harney, the oldest of her fellow photographic subjects, had been born in 1800, in the last days of John Adams’s presidency. The collective lifespans embodied in Gardner’s photograph cover more than half of the nation’s history. In traversing the long, convoluted trail to Sophie, we are fortunate to have a guide as indefatigable as Professor Sandweiss. The Girl in the Middle: A Recovered History of the American West. By Martha A. Sandweiss. Princeton University Press, 351 pages.

According to a contemporary reporter: “The Judge’s educational advantages were certainly very limited and he never improved himself much by study, for he had but little relish for books, and his knowledge of the law was very superficial.” He also “had a taste for fights” and would “adjourn his court to go watch a good one.” Harney was acquitted. Alexander Gardner was not the first photographer to visit Fort Laramie. Two years earlier, an idealistic Quaker named Ridgeway Glover had arrived. Convinced that the Indians would not harm so earnest a visitor, he defied the locals’ warning and wandered outside the Fort alone. His body was discovered later. Reports differed on whether he had been beheaded, disemboweled, or burned, but all agreed that he had been scalped. By coincidence, one of the soldiers who found Glover’s corpse was a Civil War veteran named Posey Ryan. A decade later, he would meet and marry Sophie, who bore him five children. Ryan left Sophie for another woman – taking all five children with him. Sophie was fortunate. After marrying the woman for whom he left Sophie, Ryan later quarreled with her over money, and shot her and a step-daughter dead in a restaurant. “I didn’t have the slightest idea of killing them when I went into the restaurant,” Posey told a friend. “But … I was mad.” What of Sophie herself? She remarried, this time to a mixed-race medicine show performer, who later served as a translator for prominent anthropologists. Sophie bore him eight children. Having brought a total of 13 children into the world, she lived out her life on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota, where she found work as a laundress at a boarding school. She took advantage of her location to learn to read and write. This is not a book for the genteel or delicate. The Indians are no more idealized than the white invaders. In 1906, Sophie’s father, embittered by Indian raids on his business, told an interviewer that the Indians “ought to be killed and burned as the whites were by them.” His Indian daughter’s reaction to this grim opinion is not reported. Nor is this a book for advocates of “intersectionality.” Minorities did not find common cause with each other. A peace commissioner’s wife hears Frederick Douglass declare that black people deserved civil rights more than Indians, because “the negro is more like the white man than the Indian in his tastes and tendencies, and disposition to accept civilization.” Professor Sandweiss narrates her story in an easy, friendly manner. She is not above leavening her reporting with literary flourishes now and then. Describing Sophie’s death, she writes: “She passed away in her simple dugout home alongside a trout stream. The bearskin hanging over her front door flapped in the winds blowing from the west.” Perhaps the bearskin flapped, but that’s prose, not history. In an age when lives were nasty, br utish, and short, Sophie’s longevity is astonishing. She survived poverty, wars, massacres, and natural disasters to live to 1936, midway through Franklin Roosevelt’s second term. General Harney, the oldest of her fellow photographic subjects, had been born in 1800, in the last days of John Adams’s presidency. The collective lifespans embodied in Gardner’s photograph cover more than half of the nation’s history. In traversing the long, convoluted trail to Sophie, we are fortunate to have a guide as indefatigable as Professor Sandweiss. The Girl in the Middle: A Recovered History of the American West. By Martha A. Sandweiss. Princeton University Press, 351 pages.
